lines: The shop's own benchmark from last time came back looking wonderfully clean, a flat, even latency distribution with no hot spots anywhere in sight.
That very same week, the shop's real traffic told a completely different story, with a tiny sliver of customers generating nearly a third of every single lookup.
One tidy benchmark. One real traffic shape that benchmark never actually looked like.
So what exactly did that benchmark's own data get wrong, and what single change to how it was generated would actually fix it.
Was the query itself somehow broken, or was something else entirely to blame.
answer: What was wrong was the data feeding it. Picking a customer id uniformly at random spreads load evenly across every single customer, which real traffic simply never does.
Swap that for a seeded, skewed generator instead, and the real hot-key shape comes right back on the exact same query.

lines: Here is that same uniform baseline, confirmed.
Same query, same load shape, a customer id picked uniformly at random. Every customer carries roughly the same number of orders, and the lookup runs equally fast no matter who you ask for.
Now swap in a seeded, skewed generator, and change absolutely nothing else about the query or the load.
Suddenly, one busiest customer is carrying a wildly disproportionate share of all the orders.
And looking that customer up takes measurably longer than looking up anyone else. The hot key was sitting there the entire time. The uniform data was simply hiding it.
A query planner that assumes every column is independent of every other one runs into real trouble here.
Make two columns genuinely correlated, say one deciding the other outright, and that planner's own row-count estimate comes out badly wrong.
Run the identical query shape over two columns that are truly independent instead, and the very same planner's estimate lands far closer to the truth.
Next, the dataset's own size gets stated plainly, as an actual number, rather than left for anyone to guess at.
That is exactly the same convention an entire industry's own benchmark standards lean on, so that one person's result can be honestly compared against someone else's.
Finally, the very generator that produced both the skew and the correlation gets committed as a real, reusable piece of code, not thrown away after one run.
Give it that same seed again, run it twice, completely separately, and it produces byte for byte identical data both times.
That is what actually makes a benchmark's own data reproducible by anyone else who picks it up later.
Pulling this together now.
Uniform data quietly hides both a hot key and a correlation that breaks a cardinality estimate.
A seeded, skewed generator, an explicit stated size, and a committed, reproducible generator together turn a toy benchmark into something that actually resembles the real thing.
A benchmark comes back reporting a perfectly clean result, measured entirely on synthetic data built from independent, uniformly random columns.
Should that clean result be trusted for a real production workload, one whose actual columns are skewed and correlated.
answer: Not without running it again on data that actually looks like the real thing.
A clean result on independent, uniform data is not really a result about production at all. It is only ever a result about independent, uniform data.

This very lesson just showed both of those failure modes directly: a hot key completely invisible under a uniform key, and a cardinality estimate that only breaks once the columns underneath it are genuinely correlated.
